source_refs.note: Topic 18.6.2 (PDF 102-103); Figure 18.11 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: During gamete formation, in meiosis I, homologous chromosomes go through crossing over, which is responsible for the recombination of linked genes. The chromatids of the two homologous chromosomes line up next to one another and swap (exchange) sections of DNA; the DNA strands actually break and re-join. Afterwards the homologous chromosomes separate.

blocks.alt: Four stages, each chromatid carrying genes A, B and C. 1, Homologous chromosomes: an orange chromosome (two sister chromatids A B C, same alleles) and a purple one (a b c). 2, Pairing and exchange of segments: the inner non-sister chromatids (same genes, different alleles) swap the segment with C and c. 3, Homologous pair separates. 4, Chromatids separate and each enters a gamete: A B C and a b c are parental combinations; A B c and a b C are new combinations.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.11: Crossing over (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.11).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Sister chromatids, Same alleles; Non-sister chromatids, Same genes, different alleles; Homologous chromosomes; Pairing and exchange of segments; Homologous pair separates; Chromatids separate & each enters a gamete; Parental combination; New combinations.

blocks.text: The chromatids involved still carry the same genes in the same order, but their alleles are rearranged. When these recombinant chromatids go to different gametes a wide variety of gametes is produced, so crossing over leads to recombination of genes and is a source of genetic variability.
